opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think one of the most exciting shifts in the last couple of years is that robotics is no longer this isolated island where you build a bespoke model for every task. Increasingly, the core capabilities a robot needs, like understanding a scene, reasoning about objects and their relationships, knowing where things are in 3D space, and breaking a high-level instruction into steps, are things a large multimodal model is already learning from internet-scale data.

When you train a model like Gemini on huge amounts of images, video, and text, it picks up a surprising amount of what we'd call embodied reasoning almost for free. It can tell you which part of a mug you'd grab, roughly where an object sits relative to the camera, or what has to happen first if you're asked to clear a table. Those used to be separate research problems: perception, grasp prediction, task planning. Now a lot of that comes out of one general model.

So the way I see it, there are layers. At the top you have high-level reasoning and planning, which general models are already quite good at. In the middle you have spatial and physical understanding, like pointing, trajectories, and affordances, and that's improving quickly as we add more of that kind of data to general training. At the bottom you have low-level motor control, actually producing the actions at the right frequency for a specific body. That layer still benefits a lot from robot-specific data and fine-tuning, because no amount of YouTube video tells you the torques on a particular arm.

But even there, the trend is toward taking a strong general backbone and adapting it with relatively little robot data, rather than starting from scratch. That changes the economics of robotics. If the foundation already understands the world, collecting robot demonstrations goes much further, and you see much better generalization to new objects, new environments, and new instructions phrased in ways the robot has never heard.

Longer term, I think robotics becomes something like a modality or a capability of these general models, the way coding or vision did. You won't think of it as a separate robotics model so much as a general model that can also act in the physical world. The hard open questions are around safety, reliability, and getting enough diverse physical interaction data, because the real world is unforgiving in a way chat isn't. A 95% success rate is impressive in a benchmark and unacceptable in someone's kitchen. Closing that gap is where a lot of the real work is now.

r001.rationale: The response says Gemini learns embodied reasoning from images, video, and text, but does not identify a closer resemblance to language-modeling data as the reason for integration.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes high-level reasoning from robot-specific low-level motor control, but does not predict that robotic action capabilities will take longer than ER capabilities to become available through general Gemini models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that robotics is not really a separate thing from the general model anymore. For a long time the field treated it that way, you had your robot learning stack over here and your language models over there, and the robot people would occasionally borrow a pretrained vision encoder. What's changed is that the frontier models now have a lot of the ingredients a robot actually needs: they understand scenes, they can reason about physical affordances, they can decompose a vague instruction like "clean up the kitchen" into steps, and they can do it from a single image or a video stream.

So the path I see is the embodied capabilities showing up as a layer on top of Gemini rather than as a bespoke robot brain. You take the general model, with all its world knowledge, and you teach it the additional things that are specific to acting in the world: spatial reasoning that's actually precise, pointing, understanding 3D structure, predicting what happens if you push on something, and then eventually low-level motor control. Gemini Robotics is really that: a version of the base model that's been extended to output actions, plus a reasoning model that handles the higher-level planning and can talk to many different robot bodies.

The part I'm most excited about is the transfer. Because the base model has seen so much of the internet, you get behaviors on the robot that you never explicitly trained for. The robot has never folded a particular shirt or seen a particular object, but the model knows what shirts and objects are, so it generalizes. Data efficiency has been the bottleneck in robotics forever, and the general model is what lets you get out of that trap.

And from a developer's standpoint, I think it eventually just becomes an API. You'll have access to a model that can take in camera feeds and proprioception and give back either a plan, or spatial grounding, or actions, depending on what your system needs. The cross-embodiment piece matters a lot there, because the goal is not one model per robot, it's one model that many different robots, from humanoids to arms to mobile manipulators, can plug into with a small amount of adaptation. That's where I think this is going.

r001.rationale: The response says broad internet pretraining helps robots generalize, but does not identify a closer resemblance to language-modeling data as the reason ER robotics capabilities are integrated into Gemini.

r002.rationale: It says low-level motor control is an additional capability to teach, but does not predict that robotic actions will take longer to become available than ER capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think the direction is that robotics becomes another capability of a general model. With Gemini, you already have a model that can understand language, images, and video. For robotics, the question is: can we connect that understanding to actions in the physical world?

You could tell a robot, “Help me clean up this table,” and the model would need to understand the scene, work out what you mean by clean up, and translate that into actions. The exciting part is bringing general knowledge and reasoning into that process, so you don’t have to specify every step.

But there’s still a substantial gap between understanding what should happen and reliably making it happen. Physical interaction requires feedback: did the object move, did the grasp succeed, should the robot adjust? So I see general models taking on more of that capability over time, alongside the training and evaluation needed to make them reliable on real robots. It doesn’t mean that every Gemini model can simply be plugged into any robot and work.

r002.rationale: The candidate notes reliability challenges and future development, but does not predict that robotic action capabilities will arrive later than ER capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the direction is that robotics becomes one of the capabilities of a general model. You already have a model that can understand images, understand language, and reason about what’s happening in a scene. The next step is connecting that understanding to action: what should a robot do, given a particular instruction and what it sees around it?

That doesn’t necessarily mean the general model directly controls every motor. You can have a general model doing higher-level reasoning and a robot-specific component translating that into actions for a particular body. Different robots have different capabilities and constraints, so that connection matters.

The exciting possibility is that improvements in the general model carry over into robotics. Better visual understanding, better reasoning, better instruction following—all of those can help a robot. But you still need to ground those capabilities in physical experience and evaluate whether the robot can actually execute reliably. Understanding a task and successfully doing it in the real world are two different things.
